newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Violence in Albania - chronology of unrest.
newsitem.headline: Violence in Albania - chronology of unrest.

text.p: The following is a chronology of key events in Albania, Europe's poorest country, where new Prime Minister Bashkim Fino said on Wednesday he wanted to meet with the rebels.
Civil violence first erupted in January during mass protests by people who had lost their life savings in failed pyramid investment schemes.

Jan 16 - The government seizes 25.5 billion leks ($255 million) deposited in state-owned banks by two of the schemes. People in Vlore, 147 km (80 miles) south of Tirana, hurl stones at the city hall after a local firm postpones payments.
Jan 19 - Some 3,000 people, led by opposition politicians, break through police cordons to demonstrate in Tirana's main Skanderbeg Square.
Jan 23 - Parliament bans pyramid schemes and imposes a minimum jail term of 20 years for those trying to run them.
Jan 24 - Around 5,000 people go on the rampage in the southern town of Lushnje.
Jan 25 - Demonstrators attack Foreign Minister Tritan Shehu in Lushnje.

Jan 26 - Protests spark the worst violence seen in Albania since 1991 when thousands of people converge on central Tirana and clash with riot police. Government buildings are set ablaze in towns and cities across the country.
Jan 30 - Ten opposition parties form a Forum for Democracy, vowing to continue protests. They urge President Sali Berisha to set up a technocrat government.
Feb 6 - Over 30,000 people take to the streets in Vlore, besieging the police station.
Feb 8 - Police in Tirana use batons to prevent opposition from holding rally.
Feb 9 - Enraged protesters attack Vlore police station. One person dies and 40 are injured in the fighting.
Feb 10 - Two people die of heart attacks at up to 100 are injured in Vlore in clashes between riot police and thousands of angry demonstrators.
Feb 15 - Berisha admits mistakes in handling of pyramid investment schemes but the state cannot compensate all investors.
Feb 18 - Berisha visits Lushnje and says he will scrap all taxes on the region for two years to help people recover from pyramid scheme losses.
Feb 20 - Police in Tirana use truncheons and fire live rounds in the air to disperse protesters. About 50 students launch anti-government hunger strike in Vlore.
Feb 28 - Democratic Party and main opposition Socialists hold first talks since general election last May. Socialists demand formation of technocrat government and early elections.

Feb 28 - Night-time gunbattle erupts in Vlore after people seize weapons from police armoury, at least three civilians and one secret policeman die and 22 people are injured. Secret police later say five more police were also killed. Protesters later set fire to police headquarters.

March 1 - People block road and railway line in Lushnje in support for Vlore protesters, several other road blocks set up in the south. Berisha says government will resign and Democratic Party will form successor cabinet after consultations with opposition parties.

March 2 - Rioters in Adriatic town of Sarande sack police headquarters, seize weapons, loot shops and banks. Police flee, troops desert army barracks. Four people are killed, 22 wounded by gunfire, including stray bullets, in southern Albania.

Parliament declares state of emergency to crush insurrection. 10-article law bans public gatherings of more than four people, gives security forces power to open fire to disperse crowds, imposes controls on media.
March 3 - Parliament elects Berisha unopposed for a second five-year term. It also says insurgents will be shot on sight unless they surrender their weapons by 1300 GMT.

March 5 - Army chief of staff General Sheme Kosova is dismissed, apparently for failing to ensure security at military posts stormed and looted by insurgents. Rebels seize an army tank in Sarande and set up defence line at entrance to the town.
March 6 - Berisha, backed by opposition parties, suspends military action against rebels and offers them an amnesty. Anti government forces take control of southern town of Tepelene.
March 7 - Rebels reject the amnesty offer and refuse to lay down the arms. The West urges Berisha not to re-launch a military campaign against them.
March 8 - Rebels seize last southern government stronghold of Gjirokaster and ransack the main army base after government troops flee.

March 9 - Berisha signs agreement with leaders of all political parties calling for national unity government and elections by June. He extends the amnesty to rebels by one week, but retired general Agim Gozhita, elected leader of Gjirokaster's 15-member rebel council, repeats demand for Berisha's resignation. Rebels capture the towns of Berat and Permet

March 10 - Representatives from Vlore agree to lay down their arms, saying they want swift implementation of a peace deal between Berisha and his opponents. Meanwhile the rebellion spreads to other parts of the south with Kucove, Polican and Corovode believed in rebel hands.

March 11 - President Berisha appoints Bashkim Fino, an economist from the opposition Socialist Party, as his new Prime Minister. The violence spreads into northern Albania for the first time since the insurgency began. Up to 300 people force their way into the Barracks at Bajram Curri, over 200 km (130 miles) northeast of Tirana, and seize hundreds of Kalashnikov assault rifles. It was not clear whether the looters were pro- or anti-Berisha. Several Western embassies advise their nationals with no urgent business in the country to leave.

March 12 - New Prime Minister Bashkim Fino says he wants talks with armed rebels, as the rebellion moves closer to the capital. He meets other political parties to discuss forming an interim government to oversee new elections. The move followed appeals from Italy and Greece to meet the rebels and an announcement that a European mediation mission led by former Austrian leader Franz Vranitzky was to return to Tirana on Thursday.
